report.verdict: Africa has no pan-continental GGR print; the Q3-26 "release" is a demand index (Blask, 42 markets) showing the continent down 1.9% QoQ with West Africa (Nigeria +15.6%, Ghana +21.5%) rebounding and the tail (Mali −80.8%, Rwanda −56.1%) collapsing. The only audited benchmark, South Africa, is a R74.5bn (~$4.07bn) GGR market growing 25.6% on online betting alone, while the rules elsewhere are moving toward higher fixed licence costs (Kenya KES 50m/~$388k online licence, 1-year term), broader stake/deposit-based excises (Kenya 5% of deposits, Tanzania 5% of stakes), player withholding (Kenya 20%) and payment-rail enforcement. Entry economics are deteriorating faster than demand is growing in most jurisdictions except South Africa and Nigeria.

summary: **There is no regulator-published pan-African GGR; the Q3-26 "release" is a demand proxy.** Blask's Q3-2026 ranking (published 20 Oct 2026 via Findmore Africa) sums a search/visibility-based "Blask Index" across 42 African markets for Jul–Sep 2026: aggregate demand −1.9% QoQ after a steeper Q2 slide, with 20 markets up and 22 down. It is not GGR, NGR or stakes and must be read as direction of travel only.

**West Africa led the partial recovery; the frontier tail collapsed.** Nigeria +15.6% and Ghana +21.5% QoQ grew together for the first time since the Q2 downturn; Kenya +5.5% after a flat Q2; Ethiopia +40.9% off a licence-revoked base; South Africa −0.8%. Fallers: Mali −80.8%, Rwanda −56.1%, Tunisia −30.6%, Angola −15.6%, Mozambique −5.8%.

**Brand demand is concentrated and the top two are flat.** betPawa (Index 252.6m, 24 markets, −2.2% QoQ) and Betway (215.7m, 30 markets, +0.2%) account for 51.3% of the top-20 Index (52.1% in Q2); the top five take ~74% (our calculation). The betPawa–Betway gap narrowed from 20.1% to 17.1%. SportyBet (+13.9%, #3), Bet9ja (+14.9%) and SportPesa (+26.2%, Kenya +33.1%) captured the Nigerian/Kenyan rebound; Premier Bet −33.3% on a 77% Mali collapse.

**South Africa is the only audited, regulator-published market and it is large.** NGB's FY2024/25 summary (1 Apr 2024–31 Mar 2025, published Apr 2026): turnover R1.50tn (~$82bn) +30.7%; GGR R74.5bn (~$4.07bn) +25.6%; taxes/levies R5.81bn (~$0.32bn) +20.1%. Post-pandemic four-year average GGR growth is 34.1% vs 5.9% pre-pandemic.

**SA is now a betting market, not a casino market.** Betting GGR R52.0bn (~$2.84bn) +44.7% = 70% of GGR (60% a year earlier); bookmakers' sports betting R47.9bn (~$2.62bn) +49.3%; bookmakers' horse racing R3.5bn (~$0.19bn) +12.3%; totalisator GGR R0.57bn and shrinking. Casinos R16.6bn (~$0.91bn) −4.1%, LPMs R4.1bn (~$0.23bn) −0.04%, bingo R1.7bn (~$0.09bn) −8.6%.

**SA online penetration is already mature-market level.** In the six provinces that disaggregate, online betting GGR was R44.5bn (~$2.43bn) = 86% of betting GGR; NGB estimates ~60% of all SA gambling GGR is online, and notes this is understated because non-reporting provinces are booked as retail.

**SA tax is provincial, GGR-based and low.** Total taxes/levies R5.8bn = 7.8% of GGR; betting R3.42bn (~$0.19bn, +41.8%) = 6.6% of betting GGR; casinos R1.72bn (~$0.09bn) = 10.3%; LPMs 12.7%. Mpumalanga (41%) and Western Cape (37%) host most online bookmaker GGR — a provincial licensing/tax arbitrage. National Treasury's 2025 discussion paper on a national online gambling tax [seen at snippet level only] is the structural swing factor.

**SA licence counts are consolidating.** Operational bookmakers fell 7.1% to 315 (outlets up 11.9% to 594); 36 casinos operate against a 41-licence cap; 15,743 LPMs and 13,452 EBTs. Bookmaker licences are unlimited in several provinces subject to market demand/viability, so entry is possible but the demand curve is flattening (Blask SA −0.8% QoQ; Hollywoodbets absorbing local demand; Betway SA −2.9%).

**Kenya has rebuilt its regime and repriced entry.** The Gambling Control Act 2025 created the Gambling Regulatory Authority (GRA, replacing BCLB). The Gambling Control (Licensing) Regulations 2026 (LN 111, gazetted 29 Jun 2026) set the online bookmaker and online casino licence fee at KES 50m (~$388k) versus KES 8m/6m in the March draft, plus KES 5m (~$39k) application, KES 5m annual operating fee and KES 12.5m (~$97k) renewal; online lottery KES 20m (~$155k). Term cut from 3 years (draft) to 1 year; gambling capital for an online bookmaker KES 100m (~$775k); a 6% levy on advertising spend (draft 10%); the hybrid multi-product licence was removed.

**Kenya's fees are sub judice.** JR E251/2026 (Owuor & Brance v Prime CS, GRA, AG; AGOK and Safaricom interested parties): full stay 20 Jul; narrowed 7 Aug to the fee (Second) and capital (Third) Schedules; 24 Aug the court allowed GRA to collect fees (refundable if struck down) after 246 applications stalled; legacy licences expired on the 60-day transition deadline (28 Aug); judgment due 2 Oct did not land and the matter was listed for mention on 12 Oct — unresolved at 21 Oct 2026.

**Kenya's tax base widened on 1 Jul 2026.** Finance Act 2026 keeps betting and gaming excise at 5% but moves the base from wallet-based charging to all amounts deposited for betting/gaming (horse racing exclusion removed); reintroduces 20% withholding tax on winnings (resident and non-resident) and redefines 'withdrawals' so WHT bites when funds are credited to the player account, closing the re-bet deferral loophole. The standing 15%-of-GGR betting/gaming tax was not re-verified this cycle. KRA betting taxes FY2025/26: KSh16.53bn (~$128m) +24.9%, 115.9% of the KSh14.26bn (~$110m) target; WHT on betting/gaming +59.2%.

**Kenya enforcement is wired through payments and data.** LN 112 (Conduct of Gambling Operations) requires GRA approval for any payment service provider to process gambling payments (revocable), pre-trading integration with KRA's system and GRA's central monitoring system, declaration of every paybill, and player data stored/processed on servers in Kenya unless exempted. Safaricom's M-Pesa paybill switch (58 paybills cut in Apr 2025) is the de facto enforcement tool.

**Nigeria has gone sub-national.** The Supreme Court (22 Nov 2024, AG Lagos v AG Federation) struck down the National Lottery Act 2005; NLRC is confined to the FCT (FCTA-LRO); the President declined assent to the Central Gaming Bill 2025. The Federation of State Gaming Regulators (FSGRN, 20+ states) adopted the Universal Reciprocity Certificate on 7 May 2025 covering online sports betting, online casino, public online lottery and promotional competitions; 2025 fees were waived for transitioning NLRC licensees and normal fees resumed 1 Jan 2026. Non-member states remain a legal gap; no regulator-published GGR, fee schedule or tax take could be verified this cycle (n/a).

**Ghana is the fastest-growing large market on demand but fiscal creep continues.** Blask Ghana +21.5% QoQ (Betway +24.2%, SportyBet +28.1% in-market). The 10% withholding tax on winnings was repealed in 2025 and GGR is taxed at 20% [both snippet-level, unverified]; trade press on 20 Oct 2026 flagged a 20% VAT on digital services affecting online betting [unverified].

**Tanzania moved to a stake-based excise.** A 5% excise duty on betting stakes was introduced in the FY2026/27 budget from July 2026, targeted to raise TZS74.5bn (~$29m) [trade-press reports of the budget; not verified against the Finance Act]. betPawa's Tanzania demand fell in Q3; SportPesa added a small lift.

**Ethiopia is a regulatory vacuum, not a market.** The Ethiopian Lottery Service revoked all sports-betting licences in Dec 2025 and signalled in Sep 2026 a stricter relaunch of sports betting and digital lotteries with no published timetable; an audit cited a Birr 27.5bn revenue gap [snippet-level]. Q3 demand +40.9% reflects grey-market and public-debate activity, not licensed turnover.

**Payments reality: mobile money is both the rail and the regulator's lever.** Kenya (M-Pesa paybills), Tanzania and Uganda run on mobile money; South Africa runs on cards/EFT/vouchers under provincial rules. Where the regulator can switch off a paybill, licence compliance is enforced in hours, not months — a key design consideration for any PSP stack.

**Responsible-gambling and advertising rules are tightening in step.** Kenya now levies 6% of advertising spend and has separate 2026 regulations on advertising, conduct, foreign-based operators and an appeals tribunal; NGB flags rising problem gambling and intensified awareness/enforcement in SA; Ethiopia's relaunch is framed around stricter controls.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** Three tiers: (i) South Africa — large, measurable, low effective tax (6.6% of betting GGR), 86% online, but growth decelerating (betting GGR growth 53%→51%→45% over three years) and a national online tax under discussion; (ii) Kenya — ~$0.5m of year-one fixed fees for an online book, 5%-of-deposits excise, 20% WHT and 15% GGR tax, with fee legality unresolved — a consolidation market; (iii) Nigeria/Ghana — strongest demand recovery but state-by-state licensing (Nigeria) and VAT/levy creep (Ghana). Frontier markets (Mali, Rwanda, Ethiopia) demonstrate single-event regulatory risk that can erase 50–80% of demand in a quarter.

segments.name: Demand & operator landscape (Blask Q3-26, 42 markets)
segments.headline: Continent −1.9% QoQ; West Africa rebounds, frontier tail collapses; betPawa and Betway hold 51% of top-20 demand but are not growing.
narrative: Blask's Q3-2026 edition (July–September, published 20 Oct 2026) uses the same 42-market set and the same data pull for both quarters, so the quarter-on-quarter comparison is internally consistent even if the index itself is a demand proxy built from open-source signals rather than reported GGR. Aggregate demand across the 42 markets fell 1.9% QoQ, a marked deceleration from the Q2 slide; 20 markets grew and 22 fell. The gainers list is led by small bases — Sudan +52.3%, Ethiopia +40.9%, Sierra Leone +36.1% — but the absolute weight sits with Ghana +21.5% and Nigeria +15.6%, which grew in the same quarter for the first time since the Q2 downturn. Kenya +5.5% and Uganda +1.3% stabilised; DR Congo +4.2%; Botswana +11% and Zimbabwe +9.9% extended a Southern African recovery that South Africa itself did not share (−0.8%).

The brand table is dominated by two multi-market operators. betPawa's Index was 252.6m across 24 countries (−2.2% QoQ) with declines in Tanzania, Uganda and Cameroon partly offset by DR Congo and Zambia; Betway was 215.7m across 30 countries (+0.2%), rotating out of South Africa (−2.9%) into Ghana (+24.2%) and Mozambique (+5%). Together they hold 51.3% of the top-20 Index (52.1% in Q2) and the gap between them narrowed from 20.1% to 17.1%. Our own aggregation of the top-20 gives a combined Index of 912.2m, +0.3% QoQ — essentially flat — with the top five at roughly 74%. The commercial read is that the continent's two broadest footprints have stopped compounding and growth is being captured by country specialists.

The growth cohort is Nigerian and Kenyan. SportyBet (+13.9% to 91.7m, 22 markets) rose on Nigeria +16.9% and Ghana +28.1%; Bet9ja (+14.9% to 33.9m) on Nigeria +14.8%; SportPesa (+26.2% to 18.6m) almost entirely on Kenya +33.1% with a smaller Tanzanian lift; Fortebet (+14.4%) on Uganda +14.7% in a market that was only +1.3% overall. Betika (+5.7%) recovered modestly in Kenya (+2.5%) after a sharp Q2 drop. None of these has a second market large enough to offset its home market, so their trajectories are effectively single-country bets on Nigerian and Kenyan regulatory stability.

The decliners illustrate how a single jurisdiction can swing a multi-market operator. Premier Bet (−33.3% to 22.0m across 22 countries) lost 77% of its Mali line as that market fell 80.8%; Elephant Bet (−10.2%) shed demand in Mozambique and Angola, its two largest markets; Rwanda's 56.1% market decline hit Fortebet's non-Ugandan lines. In South Africa, single-country brands YesPlay (−8.8%) and Lotto Star (−6%) gave back Q2 gains as the market flattened while Hollywoodbets (+1.1%, 76.4m) continued to absorb local demand. MWOS and Betclic entered the top 20 as bet223 and 888bet dropped out; 1xBet is present in all 42 markets but only ranks 12th (16.5m), indicating a thin, broad grey-to-licensed footprint rather than depth anywhere.

For an operator weighing entry, the index says three things: (1) the continent is not growing in aggregate on a demand basis in 2026, so share must be taken rather than ridden; (2) Nigeria and Ghana are where incremental demand is appearing, and the leaders there (SportyBet, Bet9ja, Betway) are local-content and local-payment specialists; (3) exposure to small francophone and East African frontier markets carries a demonstrated 50–80% single-quarter demand drawdown risk when licensing or payment access changes.

segments.name: South Africa — the audited benchmark (NGB FY2024/25)
segments.headline: R74.5bn (~$4.07bn) GGR +25.6%, driven entirely by online sports betting (+49.3%); land-based in decline; effective tax 7.8% of GGR with a national online tax under discussion.
narrative: The National Gambling Board's FY2024/25 summary (1 April 2024–31 March 2025, compiled from audited provincial licensing authority submissions under s.65 of the National Gambling Act 2004 and published April 2026) is the only regulator-audited GGR series on the continent. Turnover reached R1,500.7bn (~$82.0bn), +30.7%; GGR R74.5bn (~$4.07bn), +25.6%; taxes and levies R5.81bn (~$0.32bn), +20.1%. Quarterly GGR ran R17.3bn, R18.1bn, R20.1bn and R19.1bn through the year (vs R13.8bn–R15.7bn the prior year), so Q4 FY24/25 (Jan–Mar 2025) was already below Q3 — the first sign of a plateau that Blask's flat Q3-26 SA demand reading corroborates. The NGB itself describes a structural post-COVID shift: average GGR growth of 34.1% in the four post-pandemic years against 5.9% before.

Growth is wholly a betting story. Betting GGR (bookmakers plus totalisators) was R52.0bn (~$2.84bn), +44.7%, lifting its share of GGR from 60% to 70%; betting turnover was R1,125.6bn (~$61.5bn), +47.9%, implying a blended hold of 4.6%. Within betting, bookmakers' sports betting GGR was R47.9bn (~$2.62bn), +49.3% (after +55.3%, +61% and +57% in the three prior years — decelerating but still compounding); bookmakers' horse racing R3.5bn (~$0.19bn), +12.3%; totalisator horse racing R0.34bn (−10.6%) and totalisator sports R0.23bn (−9.8%) continue to shrink. Casinos fell 4.1% to R16.6bn (~$0.91bn), LPMs were flat at R4.1bn (~$0.23bn) and bingo fell 8.6% to R1.7bn (~$0.09bn). In the six provinces that disaggregate channel (WC, MP, LP, NW, EC, NC), online betting GGR was R44.5bn (~$2.43bn), 86% of betting GGR, and NGB estimates ~60% of all SA GGR was online — explicitly understated because non-reporting provinces are booked entirely as retail. The casino share of GGR has fallen from 81.9% in FY2010/11 to 22.3%.

The licensing map explains the provincial skew. Bookmaker licences are issued provincially — unlimited in the Western Cape, Mpumalanga, Limpopo, Northern Cape and Free State subject to market demand and viability, capped at 131 in Gauteng, 48 in KZN and 19 in North West — and online bookmakers have clustered where the regulator and tax regime are most accommodating: Mpumalanga generated 41% of betting GGR (R21.3bn) and 54% of betting turnover, the Western Cape 37% (R19.5bn), while Gauteng, the population centre, took only 9%. Operational bookmakers fell 7.1% to 315 (Gauteng 140, Mpumalanga 52, Western Cape 47) while outlets rose 11.9% to 594 and totalisator outlets to 366; 36 of a maximum 41 casino licences are operating after Mayfair Casino (Eastern Cape) closed in January 2025. Consolidation at the licence level alongside 45% GGR growth tells you scale economics in marketing and payments are already biting.

Tax is provincial, GGR-based and comparatively light. Taxes/levies of R5.8bn equal 7.8% of GGR; betting contributed R3.42bn (~$0.19bn), +41.8%, or 6.6% of betting GGR (59% of all gambling tax), casinos R1.72bn (~$0.09bn, 10.3% of casino GGR, −2.9%), LPMs R0.53bn (12.7%) and bingo R0.15bn (8.4%). Mpumalanga (R1.40bn) and the Western Cape (R1.23bn) collected 77% of betting tax. National Treasury's 2025 discussion paper making the case for a national online gambling tax [seen at snippet level only; not read] is the single most important fiscal risk: a national layer on top of provincial levies would move SA from the lowest effective betting tax among the markets covered here toward Kenyan levels. NGB also flags rising problem-gambling consequences and intensified enforcement against illegal operators and uncertified equipment.

Commercially, South Africa is the one African market where an entrant can underwrite a plan on audited numbers: a ~$2.4bn online betting pool growing (but decelerating) at 40%+, 6.6% effective GGR tax, card/EFT/voucher payments and a provincial licence that is obtainable in the Western Cape or Mpumalanga. The counterweights are a flat demand reading in Q3-26, Hollywoodbets' and Betway's entrenchment (Blask: 76.4m and the largest Betway market respectively), the Remote Gambling policy vacuum that leaves online casino technically outside the national framework (bookmakers offer casino-style 'betting on' products under provincial rules), and the national tax debate.

segments.name: Kenya — Gambling Control Act regime: licensing, tax and enforcement
segments.headline: Entry repriced to ~KES 60m (~$465k) year-one for an online book on a 1-year term, 5%-of-deposits excise plus 20% winnings WHT from 1 Jul 2026; fee legality unresolved after the 2 Oct judgment slipped.
narrative: Kenya replaced the Betting, Lotteries and Gaming Act with the Gambling Control Act 2025, which created the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Kenya (GRA) in place of the BCLB, and on 29 June 2026 gazetted a suite of regulations: Licensing (Legal Notice 111), Conduct of Gambling Operations (LN 112), Advertising, Foreign-Based Operators and an Appeals Tribunal. The licensing schedule moved sharply between the March draft (consulted to 13 April) and the gazetted text: the online bookmaker licence fee rose from KES 8m to KES 50m (~$388k), online casino from KES 6m to KES 50m, online lottery from KES 6m to KES 20m (~$155k); the annual operating fee from KES 3m to KES 5m (~$39k); the online licence term was cut from three years to one, so the KES 50m is in substance an annual cost (renewal KES 12.5m, ~$97k); gambling capital for an online bookmaker doubled to KES 100m (~$775k), public lottery to KES 150m (~$1.16m), online bingo KES 50m; the hybrid four-product online licence was deleted; and the advertising levy was set at 6% of spend against a 10% proposal that the Association of Gaming Operators Kenya had opposed. Legacy BLGA licences stayed valid for 60 days from gazettement, i.e. to 28 August 2026.

The fee and capital schedules are under judicial review (JR E251/2026, Owuor & Brance v Prime Cabinet Secretary, GRA and AG; AGOK and Safaricom as interested parties). Justice Musyoka granted leave on 20 July operating as a stay of the whole regulations; on 7 August he refused to discharge it but narrowed it to the Second Schedule (fees) and Third Schedule (capital), returning everything else to force; on 24 August he allowed GRA to collect the disputed fees so that 246 stalled applications could proceed, with GRA undertaking refunds if the schedules are struck down (Regulation 27's non-refundability clause does not cover a quashing). Applicants also argue the regulations were signed by the wrong Cabinet Secretary (the Prime CS rather than the CS named in the draft), and the judge has flagged the applicants' standing (neither holds a licence). Judgment set for 2 October did not land; the matter was listed for mention on 12 October after interested parties and State Counsel were given time, including to review related constitutional petitions. As of 21 October the outcome is unknown: operators have paid KES 50m-scale fees under an undertaking rather than a ruling.

The tax stack tightened on 1 July 2026 under the Finance Act 2026. Excise on betting and on gaming stays at 5%, but the base shifts from the wallet-based mechanism to all amounts deposited for betting or gambling purposes regardless of whether they sit in a wallet, and the horse-racing exclusion is deleted. Withholding tax on winnings is reintroduced at 20% for residents and non-residents, and 'withdrawals' are redefined so the tax point is when money or money's worth is paid or disbursed to the player's account rather than when the player cashes out — closing the deferral that allowed winnings to be re-bet untaxed. The standing 15%-of-GGR betting/gaming tax carried over from the old Act was not re-verified in this cycle. Receipts show the direction: KRA's FY2025/26 report puts betting taxes at KSh16.53bn (~$128m), +24.9%, 115.9% of a KSh14.26bn (~$110m) target, with betting tax +20.3% and WHT on betting and gaming +59.2%, helped by real-time taxation-at-source integration with operators — betting outgrew corporation tax (+14.0%), VAT (+8.5%) and PAYE (+6.7%).

Enforcement is engineered through payments and data rather than courts. LN 112 bars a payment service provider from processing or settling gambling payments without GRA approval and lets GRA revoke that approval; a licensee must, before trading, confirm integration with KRA's tax system and GRA's central monitoring system and declare every paybill it will use; player data must be encrypted in transit and at rest and stored and processed on servers in Kenya unless GRA grants a written exemption. The precedent is April 2025, when the previous regulator ordered Safaricom to cut off paybills for 58 platforms. The practical implication is that licence suspension equals immediate loss of M-Pesa collections, and that hosting, data and tax-API architecture must be Kenya-resident from day one.

Demand is recovering modestly — Blask Kenya +5.5% QoQ in Q3 after a flat Q2, SportPesa +33.1% in-market and Betika +2.5% — but the economics for a new entrant are now: ~KES 60m (~$465k) of fees in year one (application + licence + operating), KES 100m (~$775k) of ring-fenced capital, 6% of advertising spend, 5% of every deposit, 15% of GGR and 20% of player winnings, on a one-year licence whose fee may or may not survive judicial review. That is a consolidation regime designed around the incumbents (SportPesa, Betika and the pan-African books) and squeezes sub-scale brands out; it is attractive only for an operator with an existing Kenyan customer base or a B2B route into a licensed incumbent.

segments.name: Nigeria — state-led licensing after the Supreme Court
segments.headline: Largest demand rebound (+15.6% QoQ) inside the least settled legal framework: NLRC confined to the FCT, 20+ states licensing via FSGRN's Universal Reciprocity Certificate, fees live since 1 Jan 2026, non-member states a gap.
narrative: On 22 November 2024 a seven-judge Supreme Court panel in Attorney-General of Lagos State & 21 Ors v Attorney-General of the Federation & 15 Ors unanimously held that lotteries, betting and gaming are residual matters within the exclusive competence of state Houses of Assembly, declared the National Lottery Act 2005 unconstitutional in its entirety and issued a perpetual injunction against federal implementation in any state. The National Assembly's attempt to recentralise via the Central Gaming Bill 2025 — argued on the basis that online gaming rides on federally regulated telecoms and internet services — passed both chambers but was refused presidential assent on the ground that the medium does not change the constitutional character of the activity. The National Lottery Regulatory Commission's writ is therefore limited to the Federal Capital Territory, where the FCTA Lottery Regulatory Office now licenses retail lottery, sports betting, casino, interactive gaming and telco-facilitated gaming for what the guide describes as the second-largest market after Lagos.

The operating framework that replaced it is sub-national. Lagos State's Lotteries and Gaming Authority (LSLGA, under the 2021 law) is the benchmark regulator, issuing sports betting, casino, lottery operator, gaming machine, pool betting and promotional permit licences across land-based and online channels; Rivers, Ogun and Plateau had parallel regimes before the judgment. On 7 May 2025 the Federation of State Gaming Regulators of Nigeria (FSGRN), with more than twenty member states, adopted a Subnational Reciprocity Licensing Framework whose instrument, the Universal Reciprocity Certificate (URC), authorises online sports betting, online casino, public online lottery and promotional competitions across all member states under one authorisation administered by the FSGRN Secretariat. Transitioning NLRC licensees who met the qualification criteria received a full licence-fee waiver for the 2025 licensing year; normal renewal fees and regulatory charges resumed on 1 January 2026. The URC does not cover land-based categories and has no effect in states outside FSGRN, a number of which have neither joined nor legislated — so coverage must be audited state by state and enforcement risk in non-member states takes the form of ad hoc executive or revenue action.

What is missing is as important as what is present. No state regulator or FSGRN publishes market GGR, stakes or active-player data; neither the URC fee schedule nor state-level tax rates (lottery/gaming levies, withholding on winnings under the 2025 federal tax reform) could be verified from a primary source in this cycle and are shown as n/a. The only quantified signal is demand: Blask has Nigeria +15.6% QoQ in Q3-26 after a Q2 contraction, with SportyBet +16.9% and Bet9ja +14.8% in-market and BetKing +4.3% Africa-wide — all three are Nigeria-centric brands with no second market of comparable weight.

For B2Tech the implication is that Nigeria must be approached as a federation of licences: a URC for the online products it covers, an LSLGA licence for Lagos where the regulator is most sophisticated and the market deepest, FCTA-LRO for Abuja, and a risk-tiered map of (i) FSGRN states, (ii) states with independent regimes, (iii) states with no framework. Due diligence on any acquisition must treat legacy NLRC licences as insufficient. The upside is that the market's demand recovery is the strongest of the large markets and the incumbents are local brands rather than the pan-African books, leaving room for a differentiated product; the downside is regulatory cost that scales with the number of states and the absence of any audited market data to size the opportunity.

segments.name: Ghana, Tanzania, Ethiopia and the frontier tier
segments.headline: Ghana is the demand leader (+21.5% QoQ) with VAT/levy creep; Tanzania shifted to a 5% stake excise; Ethiopia is closed pending a stricter relaunch; small markets showed 50–80% single-quarter drawdowns.
narrative: Ghana delivered the strongest growth among the large markets on Blask's measure, +21.5% QoQ, with Betway +24.2% and SportyBet +28.1% in-market; it was Betway's offset for a weaker South Africa. The fiscal backdrop as reported in trade press is a 20% tax on GGR and the 2025 repeal of the 10% withholding tax on betting winnings, with the Gaming Commission of Ghana maintaining its licensing framework through 2026; on 20 October 2026 trade press flagged a 20% VAT on digital services as affecting online betting. None of these Ghanaian items was read from a primary source in this cycle and all are marked unverified; the direction — indirect-tax creep on a market that had just removed a player tax — is the point to diligence before relying on Ghana as the growth leg.

Tanzania moved from GGR-based to stake-based taxation in the FY2026/27 budget: a 5% excise duty on betting stakes effective from July 2026, which the government reportedly targeted to raise an additional TZS74.5bn (~$29m). This was seen only in trade-press coverage of the budget and has not been verified against the Finance Act text or the Gaming Board of Tanzania's regulations. A 5%-of-stakes levy is economically severe for a sports book running single-digit hold — at the 4.6% blended hold South Africa reports it would exceed GGR — and would be expected to compress odds, promotions and the market's size; Blask already shows betPawa's Tanzanian demand declining in Q3 with only a small SportPesa lift.

Ethiopia is a regulatory vacuum rather than a market. The Ethiopian Lottery Service revoked all sports-betting licences in December 2025 and in September 2026 said it is preparing a stricter relaunch of sports betting and digital lotteries, without publishing a reopening timetable; an audit reportedly cited a Birr 27.5bn revenue gap as motivation [snippet-level, unverified; USD not converted for lack of a verified rate]. Blask's +40.9% Q3 demand reading there tracks public debate and grey-market activity rather than licensed turnover, and should not be modelled as revenue.

The tail of the 42-market set is where single-event risk shows: Mali −80.8% (Premier Bet's line −77%), Rwanda −56.1%, Tunisia −30.6%, Angola −15.6% and Mozambique −5.8%, while Uganda (+1.3%, Fortebet +14.7%) and DR Congo (+4.2%, NgeNge and Congo Bet roughly flat) were stable and Botswana (+11%) and Zimbabwe (+9.9%) continued a Southern African recovery. No regulator statistics for these markets were obtained in this cycle; the lesson for portfolio construction is that francophone and small East African markets can lose more than half their demand in a quarter on licensing, payment or political events, so they belong in an opportunistic bucket rather than the core plan.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling and advertising
segments.headline: Mobile money is both the rail and the regulator's switch; data residency and tax-API integration are now licence conditions in Kenya; advertising levies and RG obligations are rising everywhere.
narrative: In East Africa the payment stack is the regulatory perimeter. Kenya's LN 112 makes GRA approval a precondition for any payment service provider to process or settle gambling payments, with approval revocable; licensees must declare every paybill and confirm integration with KRA's taxation-at-source system and GRA's central monitoring system before trading. Safaricom's presence as an interested party in the licensing litigation — after the regulator's affidavits raised the prospect of channel deactivation and GRA gave assurances that licensed operators' paybills would stay on — confirms that M-Pesa access, not the licence certificate, is the binding constraint. KRA's +59.2% growth in withholding on betting and gaming in FY2025/26 is the fiscal dividend of that integration. Operators should assume similar architectures (real-time monitoring, tax at source, PSP gating) will spread to Tanzania and Uganda, where mobile money is equally dominant.

South Africa is the exception: a card/EFT/voucher market under provincial rules, with 86% of betting GGR online and no equivalent central monitoring system for betting (the NCEMS covers LPMs). The regulator's stated concerns are problem gambling and illegal operators; the FY2024/25 report commits to intensified awareness campaigns and enforcement to confine consumers to compliant operators and certified equipment, and NGB explicitly links the 25.6% growth to more pronounced social consequences — the political groundwork for both the Treasury's national online tax discussion and tighter advertising rules.

Kenya's 2026 package includes stand-alone advertising regulations and a 6% levy on advertising spend (the draft proposed 10%); data must be encrypted and held on servers in Kenya unless exempted. Combined with the KES 100m (~$775k) ring-fenced gambling capital, the one-year licence term and 20% WHT on winnings credited to accounts, the regime is designed to make the licensed channel fully observable to the state. For a B2B/B2C stack this means in-country hosting or an exemption, a tax API, a monitoring-system feed, and PSP contracts that survive regulatory suspension — all before the first bet.

Ethiopia's relaunch is being framed by the Lottery Service around stricter controls; Nigeria's state regulators (LSLGA in particular) attach technical and consumer-protection standards to online licences; Ghana removed a player-side tax but is reportedly adding VAT. The direction of travel across the continent is convergent: more of the value chain (payments, data, marketing) is being brought inside the licence, and the cost of compliance is becoming the main barrier to entry rather than the licence fee itself.

highlights.text: South Africa offers an audited, ~$2.4bn online betting pool (R44.5bn, 86% of betting GGR) growing 45–49% with an effective betting tax of only 6.6% of GGR and unlimited bookmaker licences in the Western Cape/Mpumalanga — the only African market an entrant can underwrite on regulator numbers.

Nigeria's demand rebound (+15.6% QoQ; SportyBet +16.9%, Bet9ja +14.8%) coincides with a now-settled constitutional position and a single multi-state instrument (URC) for online sports betting, casino and lottery across 20+ FSGRN states — the first workable multi-state licence since 2005.
Ghana is the fastest-growing large market on demand (+21.5% QoQ) and removed the 10% player winnings tax in 2025 [unverified], improving price competitiveness versus the grey market.

Kenya's KES 50m (~$388k) annual online licence, KES 100m (~$775k) capital requirement and 6% ad levy will force out sub-scale brands; an operator with scale or a B2B route into SportPesa/Betika-tier incumbents can gain share in a market whose tax take grew 24.9% to KSh16.5bn (~$128m).
The pan-African leaders are flat (betPawa −2.2%, Betway +0.2%; combined share of top-20 demand down to 51.3%), so share is contestable by country specialists with local content and payments.

Southern Africa ex-SA (Botswana +11%, Zimbabwe +9.9%) and DR Congo (+4.2%) are growing quietly with low brand concentration (NgeNge, Congo Bet single-market), offering adjacency entries from a South African base.

lowlights.text: Kenya's entire fee and capital schedule is sub judice (JR E251/2026): fees are being paid under a refund undertaking, the 2 Oct judgment slipped to a 12 Oct mention, and the wrong-signatory argument could void LN 111 — budgeting certainty is nil for FY2026/27.

Stake/deposit-based taxes are spreading: Kenya 5% of all deposits (horse racing now included) plus 20% WHT on winnings credited to accounts; Tanzania 5% of stakes [unverified] — at a 4.6% blended sports hold such levies can exceed GGR and force odds compression.

Nigeria has no audited market data, no verified fee/tax schedule, and a material number of states outside FSGRN where the URC has no legal effect — regulatory cost scales with state count and enforcement is ad hoc.

South Africa's growth is decelerating (Q4 FY24/25 GGR R19.1bn below Q3's R20.1bn; Blask SA −0.8% QoQ; bookmaker count −7.1%) while National Treasury's national online gambling tax proposal [unverified] threatens the 6.6% effective rate that underpins the market's economics.

Frontier markets can lose half or more of demand in a quarter — Mali −80.8%, Rwanda −56.1%, Tunisia −30.6%, Ethiopia closed since Dec 2025 — and Premier Bet's −33.3% shows how one geography can swing a 22-country operator.

Payment-rail enforcement (Kenya PSP approval, paybill cut-offs, data residency, tax-API and monitoring-system integration) makes licence suspension instantaneous and raises pre-launch fixed cost; expect replication in Tanzania and Uganda.

The continent is not growing in aggregate on a demand basis (−1.9% QoQ after a steeper Q2), so entry plans must assume share-taking against entrenched local leaders (Hollywoodbets, SportyBet, Bet9ja, SportPesa) rather than market lift.

forecast.intro: The Q2→Q3 bridge is a demand bridge, not a GGR bridge. Blask's 42-market index moved from a broad Q2 contraction to −1.9% QoQ in Q3-26: the West African rebound (Nigeria +15.6%, Ghana +21.5%) and small-base gains (Ethiopia, Sudan, Sierra Leone) were almost fully offset by the francophone/East African tail (Mali −80.8%, Rwanda −56.1%, Tunisia −30.6%, Angola −15.6%) and a flat South Africa (−0.8%). On the rules, the quarter's moving parts were Kenya's gazetted fee schedule (KES 50m online licence, 1-year term) and its litigation, the Finance Act 2026 tax base changes effective 1 July, Tanzania's reported 5% stake excise from July, Nigeria's first full year of URC fees, and Ethiopia's September relaunch signal.
forecast.view: Our independent view: **South Africa's FY2025/26 GGR (to 31 Mar 2026, due from NGB around Apr 2027) will show betting growth decelerating into the mid-teens-to-20% range from +44.7%** given the Q4 FY24/25 plateau and flat 2026 demand readings [estimate]; total GGR likely R85–90bn (~$4.6–4.9bn) [estimate]. **Kenya's licensed market will consolidate** — expect the number of licensed online operators to fall materially in the 2026/27 cycle as the KES 50m annual fee and KES 100m capital bite, while KRA betting receipts keep growing double-digit on the wider deposit base and account-credit WHT; the judicial review is more likely to produce a procedural remedy (re-gazettement) than a return to draft-level fees. **Nigeria's URC will become the de facto national licence** as more states join, but non-member-state enforcement and the absence of market data will persist through 2027. **Tax direction is unambiguously up and base-shifting (stakes/deposits, VAT, ad levies)**; effective tax on GGR for an online sports book will rise in Kenya, Tanzania and Ghana while South Africa's remains low until a national online tax is legislated — the single biggest swing factor for continental margins. Cost of compliance (data residency, monitoring integration, PSP gating) rather than licence fees will be the main barrier to entry by 2027.
watch: Kenya High Court judgment in JR E251/2026 (listed for mention 12 Oct 2026): fate of the Second (fee) and Third (capital) Schedules and the signatory challenge; GRA refund mechanics; number of licences actually issued for 2026/27.

South Africa: National Treasury follow-through on a national online gambling tax and any Remote Gambling Bill; NGB FY2025/26 statistics (expected ~Apr 2027) for confirmation of the betting deceleration and online share above 86%.
Nigeria: FSGRN membership growth and the published URC fee/renewal schedule for 2026–27; Lagos LSLGA and FCTA-LRO enforcement against non-URC operators; any revived federal legislation.
Tanzania: Finance Act 2026 text and Gaming Board implementation of the 5% excise on stakes; operator odds/promotion response and any shift of demand to the grey market.
Ghana: confirmation of the 20% digital-services VAT scope for online betting and Gaming Commission licence-fee changes for 2027.
Ethiopia: ELS relaunch framework, licence caps, fees and timetable; treatment of operators whose licences were revoked in Dec 2025.
Blask Q4-26 (Jan 2027): whether Nigeria/Ghana growth holds through the African football calendar and whether betPawa/Betway resume growth or continue to cede share.

report.confidenceNote: High confidence on South Africa (NGB audited FY2024/25 report read in full) and on the Kenya licensing/litigation/tax facts (regulation parameters relayed by two independent reports plus EY's Finance Act 2026 alert and KRA FY2025/26 receipts); medium on Nigeria (legal framework from a June 2026 practitioner guide; no market, fee or tax data verified); low on Ghana, Tanzania, Ethiopia and all frontier markets, where rule changes were seen only at search-snippet level and are marked [unverified]. Blask Index is a demand proxy, not GGR; Africa-wide GGR is n/a (no regulator or verified market-intelligence figure obtained). The 15%-of-GGR Kenya betting/gaming tax is standing law not re-verified this cycle. FX used (not verified live): USD/ZAR ~18.3 (approximate at the 31 Mar 2025 period end of the NGB report); USD/KES 129 (as implied by Oct 2026 press conversions); USD/TZS ~2,570 (implied by trade-press conversion); ETB not converted. Web-tool budget was exhausted before Ghana, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda and SA Treasury primary documents could be opened.
